web.title: Stabilized Nanoemulsions of Astaxanthin Esters of Known Fatty-Acid Composition
web.description:
The carotenoid astaxanthin (AST) (3,3¢-dihydroxy-4,4¢dioxo-b-carotene) (Fig. 1) is synthesized in the free form (unesterified) and as mono-and diesters in cells of the microalga Haematococcus pluvialis stressed by excessive illumination and elevated salt content [1]. Recently, this compound has attracted increased interest because AST showed various potential biological activities in vitro and in vivo [2], primarily antioxidant activity that exceeded those of vitamins C and E and b-carotene [3].

AST is used as a preventive agent that effectively stimulates immunity and exhibits hepatoprotective activity [4]. It was shown to have a positive effect on diabetes, cardiovascular diseases, and neurodegenerative disorders [2,5,6]. These compounds are difficult to use because of their poor water solubility and instability in light. AST and extract from H. pluvialis are usually used as oil extracts, which can adversely affect the drug bioavailability.

A nanoemulsion of AST esters with Tween-80 and EtOH with particles of diameter 60 nm was produced in one of them. This nanoemulsion was chemically stable for only 20 d despite its composition containing antioxidants such as ascorbic acid and vitamin E [12]. The aim of the present work was to develop stable water-soluble nanoemulsions of AST esters and determine their physicochemical characteristics.

The final concentration of active ingredient was 0.012 mg/mL. Aqueous solutions were prepared with added albumin (human serum albumin free of fatty acids, Sigma-Aldrich, USA) in mole ratios 1:1, 1:3, 1:5, 1:7, and 1:10 and without protein. Analogous samples with added butylated hydroxytoluene (BHT, 10 -4 M) (Sigma-Aldrich, USA) and ascorbic acid (10 -4 M) (Sigma-Aldrich, USA) were prepared. Stability was determined by spectrophotometry using optical absorption at 478 nm.

web.title: Production of O/W Emulsions Containing Astaxanthin by Microfluidic Devices
web.description:
Introduction Astaxanthin (3,3’-dihydroxy-β,β’-carotene-4,4’dione) is a bright red natural fat-soluble ketocarotenoid with a high degree of antioxidant activity. The presence of this pigment is due to the color of salmon and astaxanthin is found in crustaceans and microorganisms: representatives of bacteria, microalgae, and yeast [1]. Astaxanthin can be isolated from these natural sources or obtained synthetically.

However, due to its unsaturated structure, astaxanthin is sensitive to temperature, oxidation, and exposure to light during production and storage. The instability of astaxanthin causes a decrease in its biological activity, which significantly limits its use. According to the published data, encapsulation is effective for increasing the stability and bioavailability of astaxanthin: obtaining various emulsions, colloidal dispersions, suspensions, and nanoparticles.

In O/W emulsions, astaxanthin dissolves in the oil phase. Most emulsification methods, which are based on a high shear stress, such as high pressure homogenization, ultrasonic homogenization, and mechanical dispersion, are accompanied by the heating of the emulsion system during the encapsulation process, which POLYMER, BIOORGANIC, AND HYBRID NANOMATERIALS can lead to the premature degradation of carotenoids, including astaxanthin.

The aim of this paper is to study the possibility of using a microfluidic system to obtain stable O/W emulsions, the oil phase of which contains the H. pluvialis IPPASH-629 microalgae pigments, assessing the stability of the emulsions obtained, and maintaining the safety of the astaxanthin included in their composition.

web.title: Astaxanthin Extract From the Biomass of Haematococcus pluvialis: Incorporation and Stability in Different Model Food Systems
web.description:
Astaxanthin showed the best stability during storage when incorporated into nonacidified milk. Similarly, it exhibited better stability when incorporated into strong gels. Specifically, when 0.1 mg/g was incorporated in food gels of different strengths, 0.07 mg/g of astaxanthin was detected after 96 h of storage in the strong gel, compared to only 0.058 mg/g in the weaker gel.

It is mainly found as free astaxanthin in the red yeast Phaffia rhodozyma [12] and as astaxanthin esters in the green algae H. pluvialis and C. zofingiensis [4]. A study conducted on the dynamics of astaxanthin on Baltic Sea mesozooplankton communities indicated that diesters prevailed in the cold season, which is associated with the mechanism of protecting storage lipids during winter [13].

Despite being light-sensitive and prone to oxidation, it remains popular in farming and food applications. Researchers aim to develop various systems that safeguard astaxanthin from light exposure and other environmental factors. Techniques include complexing it with other polymers [18], binding it with liposomes [18], forming nanodispersions [19], emulsion systems [16, 17, 20, 21], and microspheres [22].

Moreover, astaxanthin has showed increased scavenging activity and improved solubility when it is complexed with hydroxypropyl-β-cyclodextrin [18]. Whey proteins are ideal for designing emulsion and dispersion systems containing astaxanthin as they release astaxanthin in a controlled way during gastrointestinal digestion [25]. There is a lack of information as to how incorporate astaxanthin in the real food processing and formulation setup, particularly those pertinent to the development of functional dairy products.

It therefore has a bright future to be applied in the aquaculture, poultry, food, and cosmetics industries as an additive (Higuera-Ciapara and others 2006). In nature, astaxanthin is able to be biosynthesized in higher plants (for example, Adonis) and by microorganisms including yeast (such as Phaffia rhodozyma) and algae (Haematococcus pluvialis) (Kamata and others 1987;García-Malea and others 2009;Xiao and others 2009).

Astaxanthin from P. rhodozyma is mainly in the free form. However, its successful industrial-scale production is still being developed due to an expensive fermentation and poor yield. Aquacultured H. pluvialis has a higher content (usually 2% to 3% w/w, dry weight [DW]) but in 3 different forms: free form (5% w/w), monoester (70% w/w), and diester (25% w/w) (Miao and others 2006;Sarada andMS 20101392 Submitted 12/10/2010, Accepted 2/2/2011.

It took 5 y in our laboratory to collect a number of microbial lipases, including lipases from multienzyme complexes obtained from physical-and chemical-induced mutagenesis and lipases (monomeric enzymes) cloned and expressed in the yeast of Pichia pastoris. This study was conducted to screen these lipases by the hydrolysis of astaxanthin esters from H. pluvialis extracts and to improve the conditions to increase free astaxanthin yield.

## Materials and Methods
### Materials
Dried H. pluvialis cell powder was obtained from a local supplier, Jingzhou Natural Astaxanthin, Inc., Hubei, China and extracted with 4-fold (w/v) hexane 3 times in a homogenizer. The extracts (containing astaxanthin esters) were concentrated in a rotor-evaporator under the conditions of 45 • C, -0.08 MPa, and 60 rpm. The extracts finally contained ≥5% total carotenoids (w/w) comprised of 5% free astaxanthin, 70% (w/w) monoesters, and 25% (w/w) diesters.
